opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's less about the technology than people expect. When we first sit down with a customer, the question isn't "can the AI do this?" It's "is this organization ready to trust something new in the control loop?"

We look at three things.

**Data.** Do they have historian data, and is it any good? Many industrial facilities have collected sensor data for years, but nobody has looked at it closely. Sensors drift, tags are mislabeled, and some instruments were installed decades ago and never recalibrated. Data doesn't have to be perfect, but we need enough signal for the system to learn how the plant behaves. Usually a few weeks of digging into their historian tells us a lot.

**Control infrastructure.** Can we actually write setpoints back to the control system safely? Some plants have modern distributed control systems with clean interfaces. Others run on a patchwork of PLCs from different decades. Autonomous control needs a reliable, secure path into the system, plus the ability to fall back instantly to the existing logic if anything looks off. That fallback matters. The operators always need to be able to take control back.

**People and culture, which is the most important one.** You're asking operators who have run a plant for twenty or thirty years to let software make decisions they used to make. If the plant manager and the control room team aren't bought in, it doesn't matter how good the model is. So we look for a champion on site, someone who's curious and willing to work through the inevitable bumps. We also introduce autonomy in stages. First the system just watches and makes recommendations. The operators compare those recommendations to their own judgment and build confidence. Then it moves to supervised control within tight constraints, and only then to more autonomous operation with wider bounds.

What I learned from the data center work at Google is that trust is earned through transparency and constraints. The operators want to understand why the system is doing what it's doing, and they need hard safety limits that the AI simply cannot violate. When they can see the agent respecting those limits day after day while finding efficiencies they hadn't found themselves, the attitude changes. They go from "this thing is going to break my plant" to "why did it do that? That's clever."

So readiness isn't a binary checkbox. It's a spectrum, and part of our job is to meet customers where they are and move them along it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is probably the question we spend the most time on, honestly, because the technology is often not the bottleneck. The trust is the bottleneck.

The way I think about it is that readiness is really a function of two things. One is the organization, and the other is the facility itself. On the organizational side, the thing I look for first is whether they already have a culture of measurement. If a plant can't tell you with confidence what their baseline energy consumption was last Tuesday, or if the operators are tuning things based on gut feel and a laminated sheet from 2009, they're not ready to hand control to anything, AI or otherwise. The customers who are furthest along are the ones who've already been living in their data, who have a historian that actually works, who know which sensors they trust and which ones they don't.

The second thing is whether there's a champion on the operations side, not just the sustainability or innovation side. I've seen plenty of projects where a VP of innovation is very excited, and then you get to the plant and the chief engineer is thinking, this thing is going to break my chiller and I'm the one who gets the call at three in the morning. And honestly, that engineer is right to be skeptical. Their job is uptime. So we really try to find the person whose job is on the line and make them the owner.

And then on the facility side, we look at things like: how good is the instrumentation, how well does the control system expose setpoints, how much headroom is there? There's a big difference between a facility that's running at the edge of its capacity and one that has slack. Autonomy is a lot easier to introduce when a mistake means you lose a little efficiency, not when a mistake means you trip a safety limit.

But I'd say the most important thing we've learned is that you don't ask for autonomy on day one. The pattern that works is recommendation first. The AI suggests, a human approves, and you do that for weeks or months. The operators learn what the system is thinking, and, just as importantly, we learn where the model is wrong, because it will be wrong somewhere. And then you move to closed loop with guardrails, hard constraints that the system physically cannot exceed, and a very easy way for the operator to hit a button and take it back. The readiness question kind of answers itself at that point. When the operators stop checking the recommendations because they trust them, that's when they're ready. You can't really talk a customer into that. They have to see it.

astra-6.text:
I think readiness is less about whether a customer is excited about AI and more about whether they’re willing to trust it with a real operational decision. There’s a big difference between looking at a recommendation on a dashboard and letting a system change how your facility runs.

So I’d ask: How do you operate today? What decisions are operators making? What are the constraints that must never be violated? And what evidence would you need before you’d be comfortable handing over some of those decisions?

It doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing transition. You can start with a bounded scope, give operators visibility into what the system is doing, and make sure they can take control back. Then you earn more autonomy through demonstrated performance. To me, readiness means having both a useful place to start and a team that’s willing to work through that process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think readiness is less about whether a customer is excited about AI and more about whether they have a path to trusting it. These are physical facilities, so the questions are concrete: What can the system control? What constraints does it operate within? What happens if something goes wrong? Can an operator take over?

I’d look at both technical and organizational readiness. Do they have the sensors, data, and control infrastructure? And do the operators—the people responsible for keeping the facility running—understand the system and feel comfortable with it?

You don’t have to jump straight to full autonomy. You can start with recommendations, demonstrate performance within a limited scope, and expand control as confidence grows. The willingness to do that, and to define what success looks like, is a much stronger signal than enthusiasm alone.
